title: Nuns in the Theravada
hookLine: the nuns' order died out in Theravada lands; some now revive it and some do not; both views are held in good faith

lines: A WOMAN IN WHITE, SWEEPING AT DAWN.
cards: A broom scrapes across a temple courtyard in Thailand, early, before the monks come back from the alms round. The woman holding it has a shaved head and wears white. She keeps eight precepts.

She meditates for hours. She may have lived this way for forty years. But she isn't a nun in the full sense the old texts describe, and in Thailand the main monastic body doesn't recognize full ordination for women.
Why not? It's a real disagreement, and both sides care about it deeply.

teach.b: The Vinaya tells how Mahapajapati, the aunt who raised the Buddha, asked to go forth. At first he declined. Then, with Ananda speaking for her, the Buddha agreed, and the order of bhikkhunis, fully ordained nuns, began.
Their voices survive in the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns.

teach.h: THE ORDER FADES IN SRI LANKA.
teach.b: For centuries the nuns' order flourished in Sri Lanka, and tradition says Sri Lankan nuns helped give ordination to women in China.
Then, in a time of war, the order in Sri Lanka died out, and historians find no clear record of it continuing anywhere else in the Theravada lands. Here is the knot.
The Vinaya says a woman's full ordination is given by both nuns and monks together.

teach.h: THE RULE NEEDS NUNS TO ORDAIN NUNS.
teach.b: With no Theravada nuns left, many elders conclude it can no longer be given: the rule needs nuns, and there are none. They are guarding the code exactly as it was handed down.
Others point to the nuns of East Asia, whose lineage traces back, in part, to those Sri Lankan women.
In recent decades, women have been fully ordained with their help, and communities of bhikkhunis now live in Sri Lanka and in other countries. They are guarding what the Buddha himself began.
In Thailand and Myanmar the main monastic bodies don't recognize these ordinations. Meanwhile, many women keep eight or ten precepts in white or pink robes, honored, practicing, teaching.

teach.h: TWO ANSWERS, BOTH IN GOOD FAITH.
teach.b: Both views are held in good faith, by people who love the same teaching.

how: In Sri Lanka some women are now fully ordained as bhikkhunis, while in Thailand, Myanmar and Sri Lanka many women live as precept-keeping renunciants (mae chi, thilashin, dasa sil mata) in white or pink robes; the main monastic bodies of Thailand and Myanmar do not recognize bhikkhuni ordination.

a woman who teaches meditation to monks

games.q: match the pieces of the story.
p: spoke for her to the Buddha

s: the Buddha never allowed women to ordain
the Vinaya tells how he first declined, then agreed once Ananda spoke for Mahapajapati.
the Vinaya says nuns are ordained by nuns and monks together
that's the knot: with no Theravada nuns left, many elders say it can't be given.
every Theravada country now recognizes fully ordained nuns
some women in Sri Lanka are ordained; the main bodies in Thailand and Myanmar don't recognize it.

games.q: you're a Theravada elder. a sincere woman asks you for full ordination, and there are no Theravada nuns to join the ceremony. what do you do?
o: decline: the rule needs nuns, and there are none.
ordain her with the help of East Asian nuns.
either, and elders have chosen both.
games.why: both answers are given today by serious, careful people. one guards the code as handed down; the other guards what the Buddha began.

practice: Hold in mind one woman who practiced: Mahapajapati, who asked first; Kisa Gotami, whom you met with the mustard seed; a grandmother, a teacher, or the woman in white sweeping the courtyard.
On each out-breath, if you like, silently wish her well: may she be at ease. Then let her go, and simply sit.

wordCard.voice: Bhikkhuni. A fully ordained nun: an order that began with the Buddha's aunt Mahapajapati, faded in Sri Lanka, and is being revived by some today.

orig.note: Pali bhikkhunī: a fully ordained nun, the women's counterpart of bhikkhu, one who lives on alms.

carryVoice: Your line: the question is still open. Two answers, both given in good faith. Until tomorrow.
